node.date_label: Peasants into Frenchmen (1976) · France: Fin de Siècle (1986) · The Hollow Years (1994)
node.description: A historian of modern France whose Peasants into Frenchmen interprets national integration as a late and uneven transformation. Maurice Agulhon’s substantive review recognizes the combination of transport, markets, schooling and military service, while questioning the weight assigned to deliberate republican intervention.

incident_edges.relationship: Interprets French national belonging as historically produced through uneven rural integration.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Agulhon’s substantive review843reports the thesis and questions its political periodization; not automatic adoption of the modernization label.

incident_edges.relationship: Combines markets and transport with schools and conscription as mechanisms of rural transformation.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Agulhon credits the plural account while asking whether deliberate state integration is given too much weight; the critique remains explicit.

named_group_routes.relationship: Geertz invokes Weber for an interpretive account of culture
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Primary p. 5 explicitly invokes Weber while presenting meaning as the object of interpretation. This does not make every part of Geertz’s work Weberian.

named_group_routes.relationship: is selectively read through later sociology, including Parsons
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Parsons’s selective reception mediates some modernization readings; Weber’s own account is not a simple celebratory stage model. Parsons’s 1930 preface documents translation of the revised 1920 essay; his 1964 pp. 348–349 explicitly use Weber’s bureaucracy analysis. Lipset’s 1959 definitions and conclusion make a different use, including Weber via Pipes to reject guaranteed democratization. These are specified receptions, not one shared stage model.

named_group_routes.relationship: connects capitalism, institutions, and religious meanings
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Tawney explicitly acknowledges Weber while reserving disagreement, providing a named example of reception within economic history.

named_group_routes.relationship: informs histories of domination, bureaucracy, and states
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Domination and bureaucracy supply conceptual tools; this broad link does not establish borrowing by every political historian.

named_group_routes.relationship: provides rationalization as a resource for critiques of modern domination
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Horkheimer 193–194 specifically discusses Weber’s counterfactual historical explanation; 222 cites Science as a Vocation critically. This supports particular reception, not every inherited rationalization claim.

named_group_routes.relationship: offers a comparison of state formation, monopolization, and rationalization
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Downgraded from influence: the present references support comparison more securely than a specific account of Elias’s borrowing from Weber.

named_group_routes.relationship: Bendix adapts Weber’s comparative resources to authority and citizenship
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Publisher biographical evidence explicitly identifies Bendix’s Weber engagement; the new support specifies Bendix rather than certifying every inherited Skocpol claim.

named_group_routes.relationship: Kocka adapts Weberian concepts to industrial organization and bourgeois society
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The 1999 publisher description explicitly names Weber and Marx; Kocka’s 1988 response also identifies Weber among earlier critical resources.

named_group_routes.relationship: is acknowledged and critically discussed in Tawney’s work on religion and capitalism
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Tawney names Weber in his introduction while explicitly reserving disagreement. Chapter IV note 32 makes the criticism specific: causal weighting, nonreligious thought and Calvinist/Puritan differentiation.

named_group_routes.relationship: Thernstrom draws on Weber to distinguish dimensions of social position
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The primary opening of Poverty and Progress chapter 5, p. 115, explicitly quotes Weber before examining property/savings alongside occupations. The link records named use in one study, not Weber’s origin of all quantitative history.

named_group_routes.relationship: Kocka draws on Marx alongside Weber for industrial and bourgeois social history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicit publisher support concerns analytical resources, not doctrinal Marxism or all German historians. This productive use coexists with the historical-left criticism already recorded.
named_group_routes.map_label: Kocka: Marx as an analytical resource

named_group_routes.relationship: Braudel disputes a Protestant-origin account of capitalism in his reading of Weber
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Afterthoughts pp. 65–67 emphasizes geographical shifts and social hierarchy. This records Braudel’s polemical interpretation; it does not equate the full Weber thesis with that summary or establish that religious change was historically irrelevant.

named_group_routes.relationship: Tawney questions Weber’s causal weighting and treatment of religious differences
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Religion chapter IV note 32, pp. 316–317, values the problem while questioning nonreligious omissions and Calvinist/Puritan flattening. It also rejects purely economic reduction; acknowledgment and criticism coexist.

named_group_routes.relationship: Koselleck uses Weber’s legitimacy typology to distinguish analytical categories
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 92, discusses transformation of historical political vocabulary into a scientific category. This specific example does not establish Weber as a founding inspiration of the entire program; Olsen’s introduction note 9 explicitly disputes that larger genealogy. Endpoint review 2026-10-24: the retained statement names this promoted individual; only its endpoint is repaired. Prior sources, wording and reading qualifications remain. See the individual entry and research packet for the fresh reading scope.
named_group_routes.map_label: Weber’s typology as an analytical example

named_group_routes.relationship: Schmoller and the Verein provide an institutional setting for Weber’s agrarian inquiry
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Kim’s scholarly biographical section identifies mentorship and the agrarian commission. This is a specified research setting, not a claim that Weber simply inherits every methodological position of the German historical school.
named_group_routes.map_label: Schmoller, the Verein and agrarian research

named_group_routes.relationship: Weber defends materialist historical inquiry against a particular juristic refutation
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The available Objectivity excerpt rejects the inference that legally regulated economic life must therefore be explained only by conscious legal purposes. Legal forms can persist while their practical social significance changes. This bounded defense is neither wholesale adherence to Marxism nor a complete account of Weber’s disagreements with Marx.
named_group_routes.map_label: A qualified defense of materialist inquiry

named_group_routes.relationship: Gramsci uses Weber’s account of German political personnel
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Intellectuals author noteH explicitly refers to Parliament and Government in the New Order in Germany in discussing Junker control. This is a particular resource, not agreement with Weber’s whole sociology.
named_group_routes.map_label: Weber on political personnel in Gramsci

named_group_routes.relationship: Weber questions how Knies derives economic method from its subject matter
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The opening of the1905second article selects logical problems and explicitly disclaims a full historical assessment. This particular critique coexists with Weber’s institutional debts; it does not reject all historical economics.

named_group_routes.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause of sustained growth: the “Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention” (2002 draft), which kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out” (2007 lecture); with Kelly and Ó Gráda, British workers’ human capital against Allen’s high-wage explanation (2014), and low initial wages and mechanical skills across England’s 41 counties (2023)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, read. October 2002 draft (“The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, p. 10): Enlightenment thinkers “created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention.” Max Weber Lecture (EUI, 2007, pp. 2–5): countries of the 1914 “convergence club” “were countries that in the eighteenth century were subject to the European Enlightenment. This strong correlation is not in and of itself proof of causality” (p. 2); the tightening of propositional and prescriptive knowledge “prevented the early Industrial Revolution from fizzling out and enabled it to become the taproot of modern growth” (p. 5). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.2–16.4): “the main reason for its precocity was its higher level of human capital”; against Allen’s induced innovation, “the driver of technological progress was something deeper and stronger than cheap coal and high wages”. “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (JPE 2023, pp. 60–61): their prediction “runs directly counter to the influential argument of Allen (2009a)”; the finding concerns the 41 counties of England, not Britain’s international position. The Enlightened Economy (2009) is unread; reviewing it, Harley (EH.Net, 2010, read) wondered “if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed” and found that it “seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.” Each quotation is tied to the text it comes from; the 2002 wording is not claimed for the 2009 book. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from technology because Mokyr had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to joel_mokyr and keeps its id. His theory of useful knowledge as such is drawn on joel_mokyr → technology.

named_group_routes.relationship: Develops conceptual history through the collective lexicon and distinguishes a concept’s contextual uses from the history of its subsequent transmission and transformation (1972 project; published response 1996).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The first volume’s date and joint credit are metadata; Koselleck’s 1996 pp. 59–66 and the existing Futures Past selected reading supply the methodological account. This contribution does not give him sole authorship of every lexicon entry. The Nietzsche and Weber resource arrows and his specific contribution to intellectual history retain their IDs with repaired individual endpoints.

named_group_routes.relationship: Joins interpretive understanding of meaningful social action with a requirement for causal adequacy.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own methodological excerpt, Definition and §7 read; intelligibility alone does not establish a causal account. Excerpt-based contribution, without adopting historical racial/animal asides.

named_group_routes.relationship: Explains how value-relevant selection identifies a historical problem while causal explanation still requires evidence.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own Objectivity excerpt’s cultural-significance/value-relevance paragraphs read; the theoretical resource concerns selection and explanation, not an assertion that all comparative sociology follows Weber.

named_group_routes.relationship: As Catherine Hall explains, Davidoff developed Weber’s questions about modernity, power, market position and status through a feminist account of gender and family.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Hall’s 2015 tribute says Weber probably did more than any other social theorist to frame Davidoff’s thinking. The qualified attribution and Davidoff’s feminist transformation are retained. This is Hall’s substantive interpretation, not a claim that Davidoff accepted an entire Weberian system; the complete tribute and Davidoff’s underlying books remain unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Iriye uses Weber’s nationalism as a contrasting example to show how cultural conceptions organize accounts of international relations.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: He grants its relative realism but treats it as situated ideology; no formative influence inferred. Delivered 1988; published 1989.

named_group_routes.relationship: Prost uses Weber’s counterfactual reasoning to identify and weigh historical causes.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A specified argumentative resource, with Raymond Aron separately credited in the passage. Max Weber is not Eugen Weber; no personal contact is claimed. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

sources.citation: Hartmut Lehmann and Melvin Richter, eds., The Meaning of Historical Terms and Concepts: New Studies on Begriffsgeschichte (German Historical Institute, Occasional Paper 15, 1996): J. G. A. Pocock, “Concepts and Discourses,” 47–58; Reinhart Koselleck, “A Response to Comments,” 59–70.

verification.note: Official institutional full PDF. Preface pp. 5–6, Richter pp. 7–9, Pocock pp. 47–58 and Koselleck pp. 59–66 read closely; final reply pp. 67–70 consulted for concluding context. Copyright/preface date the publication to 1996; the preface dates the symposium to December 1992. Claims are dated to the published text, not assumed identical to an uncollated oral delivery. Pocock explicitly says he does not read German and responds through Richter’s presentation. His criticism of the lexicon and his particular criticism of Skinner coexist with openness to complementary methods. Koselleck argues for interdependence, not an opposition between two homogeneous schools. Other contributions and original German lexicon entries unread, except as stated. No new direct quotations.
